title: Dynamic Equivalence
summary: **Dynamic equivalence** is a translation approach that seeks to reproduce the *effect* of the source on its original audience in the target audience, even if that requires departing from word‑for‑word form. Often framed today as **functional equivalence**.

content_html:
Dynamic Equivalence

Dynamic equivalence is a translation approach that seeks to reproduce the effect of the source on its original audience in the target audience, even if that requires departing from word‑for‑word form. Often framed today as functional equivalence.

Dynamic (Functional) Equivalence

  • Sense‑for‑sense: prioritize communicative function and reader response.
  • Natural target‑language phrasing, idiom, and register.
  • Accepts adaptation to bridge cultural distance.

Formal Equivalence (Contrast)

  • Form‑for‑form: prioritize source syntax/lexis, keep structure visible.
  • Higher tolerance for foreignness/archaism.
  • Useful for philology, law, liturgy, and close study.

Examples

  • Biblical idiom: “gird up the loins of your mind” → prepare your minds for action (dynamic: preserves intended exhortation).
  • French idiom: chercher midi à quatorze heures → overcomplicate things (dynamic); literal would be opaque.
  • Metaphor: Chinese 心 (xīn, heart‑mind) → “heart” + note or “mind/heart” depending on context; dynamic balances clarity with cultural sense.

Strengths

  • Improves comprehensibility and naturalness for modern readers.
  • Supports cross‑cultural communication by adapting culture‑bound items.
  • Aligns with skopos (purpose‑driven) translation for functional goals.

Risks / Critiques

  • Domestication: can efface foreignness and historical texture (Venuti).
  • Translator agency becomes decisive; potential semantic drift.
  • Reduced transparency for scholarly comparison.

When to Use Which?

  • Prefer dynamic/functional: public communication, pedagogy, sacred texts for lay audiences, technical instructions for safety/usability.
  • Prefer formal: legal contracts, interlinear study, philology, poetry where form itself is meaning.
  • Hybrid outputs: dynamic main text + translator’s notes; dual‑column formal rendering for study.
